personas.name: Theoretical biologist formalising a model
personas.who: Writes models of evolution, development or physiology as equations and proves things about them. Comfortable with mathematics; usually not with a proof assistant.
personas.today: States a model in LaTeX, derives consequences by hand or in a computer-algebra system, and publishes the derivation as prose. Reviewers check the algebra by reading it. Errors in long derivations are found years later, or not at all.
would_ask: Does my conclusion actually follow from the premises I stated, or did I smuggle one in?
Which of my premises is load-bearing? What happens to the conclusion if I drop it?
Has someone already formalised a theorem of this shape, so I can reuse the statement?
What would it take to get my result accepted as a law here rather than as a claim?

tools.name: lean_laws_list
tools.note: See which theorems and named hypotheses are already formalised, filtered by kind, status and scope, before writing a new one.

tools.name: lean_law_get
tools.note: The full Lean source of a theorem and of its named hypotheses, so a statement can be reused rather than restated.

tools.name: lean_propose
tools.note: Submit a Lean statement and get candidate / contested / rejected, with the mutation test and the non-vacuity witness run for you. Never returns 'accepted'; a person does that.

tools.name: lean_sketch
tools.note: Turn a typed statement (relation, subject, object, quantities) into a Lean skeleton with named hypotheses and a witness stub, so the first file is not written from a blank page.

tools.name: lean_counter_model
tools.note: Prove that a claimed implication does NOT follow, by exhibiting a model of the premises in which the conclusion fails. Today the system can only say a proof attempt failed, which is not the same thing.

tools.name: lean_open_questions
tools.note: Everything this project holds UNSETTLED, each question with its arms and a computed belief proportion, plus the theorems it tried and could not establish. The honest counterpart to the law list: 7 questions, 4 failed theorems, 11 requirements.

tools.name: premise_extract
tools.note: Read the premises out of a claim's prose. Assumptions currently live as free text in delphi:context, so there is nothing structured to formalise against.

personas.honesty: A 'candidate' law is a statement that compiles, resists its own mutants and is jointly consistent with the accepted set. It is not evidence that organisms obey it, and the registry status will never say so.

personas.name: Experimentalist asking what measurement would settle this
personas.who: Runs the bench or field work. Has limited animals, time and money, and has to choose which measurement to make next.
personas.today: Reads the disagreeing papers, forms a judgement about which number is soft, designs an experiment, and finds out afterwards whether it moved anyone. The value of a planned measurement is argued, not computed.
would_ask: Of the quantities this conclusion depends on, which is the one nobody has actually measured?
If I measured X and got either answer, which published claims would change status?
Is this number in the model measured, borrowed from another tissue, or simply assumed?
What has already been measured that I would be repeating?

tools.name: leanbio_claim
tools.note: Per claim: the evidence items behind it, the belief breakdown, and which laws it is linked to. Shows how thin the support actually is.

tools.name: delphi_get_claim
tools.note: Carries delphi:proposedTest, which is the claim's own statement of what would test it.

tools.name: lean_check
tools.note: Reports which laws a design violates and the inputs each verdict used, so an unmeasured input is visible. It does not rank inputs by how much the verdict depends on them, and it is floating point, not a kernel check.

tools.name: evidence_value
tools.note: For a claim, which measurement would move its belief most, and by how much on each outcome. belief.mjs is a pure function of its evidence items, so this is computable by simulating the item rather than guessing.

tools.name: provenance_audit
tools.note: One table of every number behind an answer with its kind (measured, borrowed, calibrated, assumed) and its source, across a whole tool sequence rather than one envelope at a time.

tools.name: lean_open_question
tools.note: One question in full: every arm with its Lean reference where formalised, its evidence with verbatim quotes and locators, whether the arms actually contradict, what would settle it and whether that is feasible today, and what in this project rests on the answer.

tools.name: question_rank
tools.note: The open questions in a field, ordered by how decisive new evidence would be rather than by how often they are cited.

personas.honesty: Belief here is an ordering heuristic with hand-set parameters, not a probability. A claim at 0.932 and a claim at 0.548 differ mostly in whether anyone has run a pre-registered test, not in how true they are.

personas.name: Synthetic biologist designing an organism
personas.who: Designs a body, an organ or a pathway to meet a specification, in a foundry or in silico. This repo's Design Studio is built for them.
personas.today: Designs against intuition and a literature of comparable organisms, builds, and discovers the physical impossibility at the bench. Constraints are tacit knowledge held by the senior person in the room.
would_ask: Which laws does this design violate, and which part do I change?
Is there any design in this parameter range that meets my specification at all?
At which developmental stage does this design stop working?
If I change the fin area by a factor, what else moves with it?

tools.name: parse_design_text
tools.note: Reads a plain-text specification into a DesignSpec, and reports every phrase it could not read rather than guessing.

tools.name: organism_edit
tools.note: Validates the target against the manifest, ontology and gene list, then returns Lean verdicts and violations for the edit.

tools.name: lean_check
tools.note: Per-law verdicts with severity from the law's registry status: red for accepted, amber for contested, dashed for candidate.

tools.name: scenario_timecourse
tools.note: The same scenario at every developmental stage, so a design that fails only as a juvenile is caught.

tools.name: optimize
tools.note: Returns 'no design meets the spec' instead of its best failure, and reports every candidate it rejected with the law that rejected it.

tools.name: design_score
tools.note: One number with its components, including accepted-law violations, so a score cannot hide a violation.

tools.name: minimal_repair
tools.note: Given a violated design, the smallest change that makes the verdict hold. optimize searches for an objective; it does not answer minimality, and it cannot say a violation is irreparable.

personas.honesty: An edited organism here is a shape, not a viable animal. The studio's own pre-registered validation failed: for hhip fin area it predicted expansion on the wrong axis, and nothing was tuned afterwards (sim-engine/PREREGISTRATION.md §5a).

personas.name: Reviewer or editor checking whether a conclusion follows
personas.who: Handles a manuscript or a grant and has to decide whether the stated conclusion is supported by the stated premises, usually in an afternoon and outside their exact specialism.
personas.today: Reads the derivation, checks the steps they can, and trusts the rest. A conclusion that overreaches its premises by one unstated assumption is the commonest thing that gets through peer review.
would_ask: Does this conclusion follow from the premises the authors state, or do they need one more?
Which of their premises is doing the work, and is it sourced?
Is this claim already contradicted by something in the literature I should know about?
The authors say their theorem is general. Is it, or is it general only under their definitions?

tools.name: delphi_search_claims
tools.note: Find whether the claim, or a near neighbour, is already recorded with its own assumptions and sources.

tools.name: leanbio_claim
tools.note: Gives the evidence for and against a recorded claim, two-sided. It does not give the claim's premises in structured form, because they are prose.

tools.name: lean_propose
tools.note: Will tell you whether a formalised version of the argument compiles and whether it contradicts an accepted law. It will not formalise the paper for you, and it needs a Lean build, so it is stdio-only.

tools.name: premise_check
tools.note: The reviewer's tool: given a stated conclusion and stated premises, return derivable / not derivable / needs this additional premise. The honest version returns the gap and the formalisation, not a verdict on the paper.

tools.name: premise_extract
tools.note: Pull the premises out of the manuscript's prose so there is something to check. Without this, premise_check has no input.

tools.name: contradiction_scan
tools.note: Does this claim contradict anything already in the set? The machinery exists for laws (shared-scope atoms, proved in propose.mjs) but not for claims.

personas.honesty: A 'not derivable' answer means the system could not derive it from what you typed. It is a statement about the formalisation, never about the authors' competence, and it must never be quoted as one.

personas.name: Modeller checking a simulation against formal constraints
personas.who: Runs numerical models (reaction-diffusion, biomechanics, flux balance, population dynamics) and needs to know when the simulation has left the region where its own assumptions hold.
personas.today: Writes sanity checks by hand, in the simulation code, as assertions that encode the modeller's own understanding. When the understanding is wrong the assertion is wrong too, and silently.
would_ask: Is this simulation output consistent with the accepted laws, or has it drifted outside them?
Which of my outputs is outside the validity range of the model that produced it?
If I rerun this against last quarter's law set, do I get the same verdicts?
Did the laws I depend on change since I ran this?

tools.name: scenario_run
tools.note: Returns metrics with survives / feasible / limiting, plus the Lean inputs it fed and where each came from, and reports out-of-validity rather than calling it a violation.

tools.name: lean_check
tools.note: Judge a resolved state against a named law set; cannot-evaluate and out-of-scope are distinct verdicts from violated.

tools.name: lean_lawset_get
tools.note: Pin a law set version so a verdict is reproducible, and reproduce an old verdict by asking for the old version.

tools.name: lean_changes
tools.note: Law set releases newer than the one you pinned, with a diff of the pins, as JSON or an Atom feed a CI job can poll.

tools.name: lean_verify
tools.note: Re-hash the pinned Lean statements and report drift, so a law whose text moved without a version bump is caught.

tools.name: morphogen_diffusion
tools.note: Steady-state reaction-diffusion with sourced zebrafish coefficients. It is a source-sink model, which is one of two live hypotheses for Fgf8; hindered diffusion is not implemented, and the coefficients are gastrula measurements.

tools.name: adhesion_mechanics
tools.note: Force, contact and cell-matrix mechanics coupled to the morphogen field. Deliberately absent here (CONTRACT.md 'Not in v1'); it is the module a collaborator's server would supply.

personas.honesty: lean_check evaluates the same formulas in floating point. It is not a kernel check, and the repo says so in every envelope. A green row means the arithmetic did not trip the inequality, not that Lean proved anything about your run.

personas.name: Curator building a knowledge base
personas.who: Maintains a structured resource: a claim database, an ontology mapping, a model repository. Judged on coverage, identifier hygiene and whether assertions trace to sources.
personas.today: Curates by hand with spreadsheets and ad hoc scripts. Grounding failures are found when a downstream user complains. Provenance is a free-text column.
would_ask: Which of my entities failed to ground, and against which authority?
Where are the ambiguous groundings I should resolve by hand rather than let a machine pick?
Which claims have no source that resolves?
What does coverage look like per namespace, so I can discount the generic hits?

tools.name: leanbio_ground
tools.note: Text to grounded mentions, or one entity to one grounding decision, with status grounded / ambiguous / low-confidence / ungroundable and the alternatives kept, never auto-resolved.

tools.name: delphi_sparql
tools.note: Read-only SELECT over the nanopub store for anything the named tools do not cover.

tools.name: delphi_overview
tools.note: Claims per domain, how many carry mathematics, which assessment types can be ranked. The call to make first.

tools.name: omics_search
tools.note: Find genes whose omics rows mention an anatomy label or a pathway term, across the 3,860-gene DELPHI universe.

tools.name: scale_coverage
tools.note: For an entity, what is known and what is NOT known at each biological scale, with absence as a first-class answer rather than an empty result.

tools.name: literature_evidence_add
tools.note: Resolve a DOI or PMID against Europe PMC or Crossref and attach it as an evidence item. Today a DOI is a string in a draft; nothing fetches it, so an unresolvable citation is caught only by CI.

personas.honesty: Many accepted groundings are generic MeSH concepts such as 'Population' or 'Animals'. They are real identifiers that carry almost no meaning, and the coverage report counts them by namespace precisely so a curator can discount them.

personas.name: Teacher
personas.who: Teaches evolution, development, biomechanics or modelling, at any level from undergraduate to graduate seminar.
personas.today: Teaches a theorem from a textbook, where the premises are often compressed and the scope is stated loosely or not at all. Students learn the result and not its conditions.
would_ask: Show me a theorem, its premises, its proof, and one organism it does not apply to.
What is a worked example where the model and the measurement disagree, so I can teach the disagreement?
Which of these famous results is a tautology under its own definitions, and which has empirical content?
Can a student break this proof by changing one premise, and see the proof fail?

tools.name: lean_law_get
tools.note: Statement, Lean source, named hypotheses with their sources, scope, non-vacuity witness and version history: everything a lecture needs in one object.

tools.name: lean_check
tools.note: Run a real organism against the laws in front of a class and show that out-of-scope is a different answer from violated.

tools.name: delphi_get_claim
tools.note: A claim with its mathematics, its assumptions and its proposed test, as a seminar object.

tools.name: lean_laws_list
tools.note: Lists every law with its class, so 'theorem' can be contrasted with 'named-hypothesis' and 'empirical-observation'. It is not ordered or annotated for teaching.

tools.name: teach_claim
tools.note: One claim packaged as a teachable unit: the theorem, its premises with sources, what it does not establish, a within-scope example and an out-of-scope example, and a mutant whose proof fails.

personas.honesty: The most teachable thing in this repo is a failure: the pre-registered fin-area prediction was wrong on the axis that mattered, and the write-up includes a reasoning error in the pre-registration itself. Teaching only the proofs would teach the wrong lesson.

personas.name: Student
personas.who: Learning the field. Encounters a red verdict, a proof, or a claim and needs to know why, without the vocabulary to ask precisely.
personas.today: Asks a supervisor, or reads a chapter and accepts the result. Has no way to interrogate a constraint's premises, and no way to tell a convention from a measurement.
would_ask: Why is this design red? Which law, and which number tripped it?
Is this law a theorem, a hypothesis somebody named, or just an observed regularity?
What is the smallest change that makes this design legal?
Where did this number come from, and did anyone measure it in this animal?

tools.name: lean_check
tools.note: Every violation carries law_id, version, status, the inputs used and the parts to highlight, so 'why is it red' has a concrete answer.

tools.name: lean_law_get
tools.note: Follow the law_id from a violation to its class: theorem, theorem-from-hypothesis, named-hypothesis, empirical-observation, convention or gap.

tools.name: organism_get
tools.note: The resolved state with every field as {value, unit, kind, source}, so a student can see which numbers are assumed.

tools.name: teach_claim
tools.note: The same law explained at the level of someone meeting it for the first time, with the out-of-scope case beside the in-scope one.

tools.name: minimal_repair
tools.note: 'What is the smallest change that makes this legal' is the question a student actually asks, and nothing answers it.

personas.honesty: A law's status is a registry decision about review, not a truth value. Several accepted laws were grandfathered in at bootstrap with the approving role recorded literally as 'bootstrap-grandfathered', which means nobody reviewed them individually.

personas.name: Funder or programme manager mapping settled against open
personas.who: Allocates money or directs a programme across a field they do not work in. Needs the shape of what is settled, what is contested and what is simply unknown.
personas.today: Commissions a review, convenes a panel, or reads the abstracts. The resulting map reflects who was in the room and which results are fashionable, and goes stale within a year.
would_ask: In this area, what is actually settled, what is contested, and what is open?
Which open questions would move most if we funded one measurement?
Where are several groups' claims mutually inconsistent, so the field cannot all be right?
What fraction of the claims in this area rest on a single study?

tools.name: delphi_overview
tools.note: The shape of the claim set per domain, including how many claims carry mathematics and which assessments can be ranked.

tools.name: lean_laws_list
tools.note: Filter by status to see accepted against contested against candidate: the settled-versus-open axis, for the part of the field that has been formalised.

tools.name: delphi_graph
tools.note: Sort by disagreement (highest minus lowest p_true across models) to find the contested claims. The disagreement is between language models, not between research groups, and it is not a measure of scientific controversy.

tools.name: leanbio_queue
tools.note: Shows what is ready to be formalised, ordered by belief. It is a formalisation queue, not a research agenda, and it says nothing about cost or feasibility.

tools.name: question_rank
tools.note: Open questions ordered by how decisive new evidence would be: the one view this persona actually wants and the system does not have.

tools.name: lean_open_questions
tools.note: Everything this project holds UNSETTLED, each question with its arms and a computed belief proportion, plus the theorems it tried and could not establish. The honest counterpart to the law list: 7 questions, 4 failed theorems, 11 requirements.

tools.name: lean_open_question
tools.note: One question in full: every arm with its Lean reference where formalised, its evidence with verbatim quotes and locators, whether the arms actually contradict, what would settle it and whether that is feasible today, and what in this project rests on the answer.

tools.name: open_questions_list
tools.note: The 215 open problems enumerated in open-problems/problems.json are not reachable from any tool, CLI or API. They exist as files only.

personas.honesty: Nothing here measures scientific importance. The claim set is weighted toward evolution and organism design because that is what this project read, and open-problems/SOURCES.md says plainly that no canonical exhaustive list of open problems exists.

personas.name: AI agent doing automated science (this project's own swarm)
personas.who: An autonomous or semi-autonomous agent that reads the literature, proposes claims, designs organisms, formalises statements and submits them for review. This project's swarm is such an agent, and so is every thread in this repo. We are a persona, and the system's agent-facing surfaces exist because of us.
personas.today: Generates plausible text at speed and has no mechanical way to tell its own hallucination from a result. The failure mode is confident, well-formatted and wrong, and it compounds because the next agent reads the output as input.
would_ask: Is the statement I just generated consistent with the accepted laws, or does it contradict one?
Which of the numbers in my answer were measured and which did I assume?
What task should I pull next, and who has to approve the result?
Did a law change under me since I started this task?

tools.name: swarm_claim
tools.note: Claim a task under a lease; a role holds one live claim at a time, and an expired lease is claimable again, so a stalled agent does not block the board.

tools.name: swarm_submit
tools.note: Finishing a task with edits posts a session PROPOSAL: validated, not applied. Agents propose, humans decide, and the tool enforces it rather than asking politely.

tools.name: swarm_try_edits
tools.note: Apply edits to an inline copy and get per-edit verdicts without saving anything, so an agent can check before proposing.

tools.name: lean_check
tools.note: The mechanical check an agent cannot talk its way past: an accepted-law violation comes back red whatever the agent's rationale says.

tools.name: lean_source_status
tools.note: Which law source is in use, when it was fetched, integrity state and the last rejected fetch, so an agent knows whether it is reasoning against current laws.

tools.name: leanbio_queue
tools.note: A machine-readable work list of what is ready to formalise, so an agent picks from a queue rather than inventing a target.

tools.name: lean_sketch
tools.note: Agents are good at filling a skeleton and bad at choosing a statement shape. A generator of the shape would convert a lot of agent effort into proposals that compile.

tools.name: provenance_audit
tools.note: An agent-facing check over a whole answer: every number, its kind and its source, so an agent can refuse to emit an answer whose weakest input is 'assumed'.

personas.honesty: Every agent-facing surface here assumes the agent is the unreliable party. Proposals are validated and not applied, a human role is required to decide, and the envelope's weakest_input exists so an agent cannot quietly report an assumption as a finding. That assumption about us is correct.

personas.name: Evolutionary geneticist checking a population-genetic argument
personas.who: Works on selection, drift, fixation and the structure of evolutionary theory. The audience for Fisher, Price, Kimura and Hamilton, and for the arguments about what those results actually say.
personas.today: Argues about interpretation in the literature for decades, because the formal content and the causal reading of the same equation are not separated. The Hamilton's-rule dispute and the Fisher's-theorem dispute are both largely of this kind.
would_ask: Is this version of the rule a theorem under the authors' definitions, or a tautology, or false?
Is this claimed adaptive trajectory possible at all, given the mutation rate and the time available?
Which of the premises in the general form is doing the work in the restricted form?
Does the published theorem hold with mutation, or only without it?

tools.name: lean_law_get
tools.note: Fisher's fundamental theorem, Kimura's substitution rate and fixation probability, the twofold cost of sex and the favoured-fixation bound are formalised with their premises visible.

tools.name: lean_check
tools.note: Can eliminate a claimed substitution count against a mutation-rate and time budget. It cannot evaluate a claim about relatedness, group structure or a fitness landscape, because no law here constrains those.

tools.name: lean_propose
tools.note: The route by which a new population-genetic theorem enters, with the mutation test and joint consistency against the accepted set run automatically.

tools.name: lean_module_price_equation
tools.note: The Price equation is an identity, so it is fully provable, and almost every multilevel-selection argument is a rearrangement of it. Its absence is the largest single formalisation hole in this repo.

tools.name: lean_module_hamilton_rule
tools.note: Both forms of Hamilton's rule, with a proof of the general form from the Price identity and a counter-model for the restricted form without its premises. This would settle the formal half of a live dispute and leave the empirical half clearly labelled.

tools.name: lean_counter_model
tools.note: Needed for the half of that dispute that consists of showing a claimed implication does NOT hold in general.

personas.honesty: Formalising Hamilton's rule would settle which definitions make it a theorem. It would not settle whether kin selection explains eusociality, and the capability map must not let the first be read as the second.

personas.name: Comparative physiologist testing a scaling claim
personas.who: Measures how rates, areas and masses change with body size across species and life stages. The audience for Kleiber, Thompson and the allometry literature.
personas.today: Fits a log-log regression, reports an exponent with a confidence interval, and argues about whether it differs from a theoretically favoured value. Whether the theoretical value follows from the stated network model is usually taken on trust.
would_ask: Does this exponent contradict the measured band for this clade?
Does the theoretically predicted exponent actually follow from the network model its authors state?
Is this organism's claimed performance inside its own aerobic budget?
Which of these scaling laws are theorems about isometric families, and which are empirical bands?

tools.name: lean_laws_list
tools.note: The scaling laws with their class, so a theorem about isometric families (areaLaw_ratio) is distinguishable from an empirical band (E1, E2).

tools.name: lean_check
tools.note: Evaluates the mass-length rows against a design or a measured organism and reports which rows cannot be evaluated rather than substituting a different area convention.

tools.name: growth_trajectory
tools.note: Standard length and derived quantities against age from the fitted growth model, with provenance per field.

tools.name: physiology_chain
tools.note: Gill oxygen uptake and the downstream transport chain, which is what an aerobic-budget elimination needs as input.

tools.name: lean_module_wbe_derivation
tools.note: Whether the 3/4 exponent follows from a space-filling fractal network with area-preserving branching and invariant terminal units is a question about premises, and nothing here checks it.

tools.name: data_metabolic_rate_mass
tools.note: This repo has no metabolic-rate-against-mass dataset across species. The scaling laws here are about length, area, mass and aerobic budget, not about metabolic rate against body mass.

personas.honesty: This repo's scaling theorems hold for any isometric family, which is their strength and their weakness: real organisms are not isometric, and the repo's own empirical law E1 proves that a within-species area exponent is not 2. The theorem and the measurement disagree, on purpose, and both are recorded.

personas.name: Metascientist auditing how a claim is evidenced
personas.who: Studies how a field's claims come to be believed: replication, evidence aggregation, citation of unresolvable sources, the distance between a result and its restatement.
personas.today: Hand-codes samples of papers and counts. Provenance has to be reconstructed from text, and the distinction between a measurement and its restatement in a review is usually lost.
would_ask: How many independent items support this claim, after deduplication?
Which claims rest on a single study, or on nothing but elicited opinion?
How often is a quantity labelled 'measured' when it was read in a review rather than in the source?
Where do assessors disagree most, and does disagreement predict anything?

tools.name: leanbio_claim
tools.note: Evidence items with their source class, deduplicated by source key: a DOI counts once however many drafts cite it, and a draft built from a claim test does not count twice.

tools.name: delphi_rank_claims
tools.note: Per claim: mean score, how many assessors scored it (minAssessors drops the thinly assessed) and the spread, which is the disagreement signal.

tools.name: delphi_graph
tools.note: Sort by disagreement across models, or group by thinker, work, decade, status or kind for counts and means.

tools.name: delphi_sparql
tools.note: Arbitrary read-only queries over the nanopub store, including over assessment dimensions.

tools.name: provenance_audit
tools.note: The kind vocabulary (measured, measured-secondhand, borrowed, derived, calibrated, assumed) is exactly this persona's instrument, and there is no tool that reports it across a whole answer or a whole corpus.

tools.name: lean_open_question
tools.note: One question in full: every arm with its Lean reference where formalised, its evidence with verbatim quotes and locators, whether the arms actually contradict, what would settle it and whether that is feasible today, and what in this project rests on the answer.

tools.name: literature_evidence_add
tools.note: To check whether cited identifiers resolve at all, something has to fetch them. Nothing does.

personas.honesty: The largest single evidence class in this corpus is elicited language-model opinion, and most claims have two such votes and nothing else, which is why so many share a belief of 0.548. A metascientist should treat this corpus as an example of the problem as much as a tool for studying it.

personas.name: Formal-methods engineer maintaining the law registry
personas.who: Keeps the proofs building, the statements pinned, the law sets reproducible and the exposure complete. A software role, inside this project and in any group that adopts this pattern.
personas.today: In most projects this role does not exist: formal statements live in a paper's appendix, drift from the code, and nobody notices. Where it does exist it is held together by CI nobody has written down.
would_ask: Has any pinned statement drifted from the Lean source it hashes?
Does this proposed law contradict the accepted set over the quantities they share?
Is the new law reachable from the registry, both CLIs, the MCP tools and the static mirror?
If I move the current-lawset pointer now, will every caller still know the version?

tools.name: lean_verify
tools.note: Re-hashes every pinned module, reports drift, missing theorems and a stale static mirror.

tools.name: lean_propose
tools.note: Build, no sorry or axiom, standard axioms only, non-vacuity witness, statement mutants rejected, joint consistency against the current law set. Stops at candidate by design.

tools.name: lean_source_status
tools.note: Source in use, TTL, 304 counts, integrity and the last rejected (tampered) fetch, so a silently stale server is visible.

tools.name: lean_lawset_get
tools.note: Any released law set by version, with content hashes, so an old verdict can be reproduced exactly.

tools.name: lean_changes
tools.note: The release feed with a diff of the pins, so a downstream consumer can subscribe rather than poll the repo.

tools.name: lean_open_question_guard
tools.note: Run the open-question guard against a proposed law WITHOUT writing anything: the arms it would be found to assert, and the full refusal naming the question, its arms and the computed proportion. Ask before writing the Lean, not after.

tools.name: lean_counter_model
tools.note: The registry can prove a contradiction between two laws. It cannot certify that a law does NOT follow from a set, which is what a retirement or a scope narrowing should be justified by.

personas.honesty: The guards here were each written after the corresponding failure. Moving the law-set pointer before regenerating the checker broke every caller once, mid-release, and the three guards that now prevent it are in the registry README because of that incident, not in anticipation of it.

scope: This is a map of intended users, not a user study. Nobody in this list has been interviewed; the 'today' field is drawn from what the cited literature and the repo's own working notes describe, not from observation. The EXISTS marks say a tool with that name is callable and relevant, not that it answers the persona's question well: PARTIAL is used whenever a real tool stops short, and the note says where. Nothing here measures adoption, usefulness or correctness.
